name: Scarring and abnormal scarring

# Scarring and abnormal scarring: Comprehensive Reference for Foundation Year Doctors

## 1. OVERVIEW

### Definition and Key Concepts
Scarring refers to the process of fibrous tissue formation that occurs as a natural part of wound healing. Abnormal scarring includes hypertrophic scars and keloids, which are excessive growths of scar tissue that can be raised, thick, and may cause discomfort or cosmetic concerns.

### Epidemiology
Hypertrophic scars and keloids are more common in individuals with darker skin types and can occur in up to 15% of surgical wounds. Keloids are more prevalent in young adults and can occur in any area of the body, particularly on the chest, shoulders, and earlobes.

### Essential Pathophysiology
Scarring occurs when the normal healing process is disrupted, leading to an imbalance between collagen deposition and degradation. In hypertrophic scars, there is an overproduction of collagen that remains within the boundaries of the original wound. Keloids, on the other hand, extend beyond the original wound site and are characterized by excessive collagen deposition and fibroblast proliferation.

## 2. RECOGNITION

### Key Symptoms
- Itching
- Pain
- Tenderness
- Discomfort

### Key Signs
- Raised, thickened skin
- Discoloration (red, purple, or darker than surrounding skin)
- Limited range of motion if located near joints

### Atypical Presentations
- Scars that continue to grow over time
- Scars that are painful or itchy long after the initial injury has healed

### Red Flags Requiring Immediate Action
- Rapidly growing scar
- Scars that bleed or ooze
- Signs of infection (increased redness, warmth, swelling)

## 3. INVESTIGATION

### First-line Investigations
- Clinical examination
- Patient history (including previous scars and healing history)

### Second-line Investigations
- Ultrasound (to assess scar depth and structure)
- Dermatoscopy (to evaluate scar characteristics)

### Specialist Tests
- Biopsy (if malignancy is suspected)

## 4. DIAGNOSIS

### Diagnostic Criteria or Clinical Decision Rules
Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on the appearance and history of the scar. Keloids are diagnosed if the scar extends beyond the original wound margins and is raised, while hypertrophic scars remain within the wound boundaries.

### Key Differential Diagnoses to Exclude
- Normal scar
- Hypertrophic scar
- Keloid
- Scar contracture
- Dermatofibroma
- Basal cell carcinoma

## 5. MANAGEMENT

### Acute Management (Emergency/Immediate Care)

#### First-line Treatments
- Silicone gel sheeting
- Pressure therapy

#### Second-line Treatments
- Intralesional corticosteroids (e.g., triamcinolone)
- Cryotherapy

#### Emergency Procedures
- Surgical excision (for keloids)

### Chronic Management (Ongoing Care)

#### First-line Treatments
- Silicone gel sheeting
- Pressure therapy
- Topical corticosteroids

#### Second-line Treatments
- Intralesional corticosteroids
- Laser therapy (pulsed dye laser)
- Radiation therapy (for severe cases)

#### Monitoring Requirements
- Regular follow-up to assess scar progression and response to treatment

## 6. DRUGS & PROCEDURES

### Drugs

#### Triamcinolone
- **Mechanism of Action**: Corticosteroid that reduces inflammation and collagen synthesis.
- **Typical Dosing Range**: Intralesional injection of 10-40 mg/mL every 4-6 weeks.
- **Key Side Effects/Contraindications**: Skin atrophy, hypopigmentation, pain at injection site.
- **When to Use vs. Alternatives**: Effective for hypertrophic scars and keloids.

#### Silicone gel
- **Mechanism of Action**: Hydration and occlusion promote scar remodeling.
- **Typical Dosing Range**: Apply to scar daily for at least 12 hours.
- **Key Side Effects/Contraindications**: Minimal; may cause skin irritation.
- **When to Use vs. Alternatives**: First-line treatment for scar management.

### Procedures

#### Surgical excision
- **What it Involves**: Removal of the keloid or hypertrophic scar under local or general anesthesia.
- **Indications**: Persistent keloids or hypertrophic scars that do not respond to conservative treatment.
- **Key Risks/Complications**: Recurrence of the scar, infection, changes in pigmentation.

## 7. PROGNOSIS & COMPLICATIONS

### Expected Outcomes
Hypertrophic scars may improve over time, while keloids have a high recurrence rate after treatment. Early intervention can improve outcomes.

### Important Complications to Watch For
- Recurrence of keloids or hypertrophic scars
- Infection at the site of treatment
- Psychosocial impact due to cosmetic concerns

## 8. FOUNDATION DOCTOR ROLE

### Specific Responsibilities and Limitations
Foundation doctors should be able to recognize abnormal scarring, initiate appropriate management, and refer to specialists when necessary. They should also provide patient education regarding scar care and treatment options.

### When to Escalate to Senior/Specialist
Refer to a plastic surgeon or dermatologist if the scar is symptomatic, rapidly growing, or if there is uncertainty in diagnosis or management.

### Key Safety Considerations
Monitor for signs of infection post-treatment, ensure proper technique during injections or procedures, and educate patients on the importance of follow-up.
